title: In L. Calpurnium Pisonem
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

passages.original: dices enim, ut es homo factus ad persuadendum, concinnus, perfectus, politus ex schola: quid est, Caesar, quod te supplicationes totiens iam decretae tot dierum tanto opere delectent? in quibus homines errore ducuntur, quas di neglegunt; qui, ut noster divinus ille dixit Epicurus, neque propitii cuiquam esse solent neque irati.non facies fidem scilicet, cum haec disputabis; tibi enim et esse et fuisse videbit iratos.
passages.english: For you will say, being a man made for persuading, elegant, accomplished, polished straight from the school: "What is it, Caesar, that makes thanksgivings, decreed so many times now and for so many days, delight you so greatly? In these men are led astray by error, and the gods pay them no heed; for the gods, as that divine Epicurus of ours said, are not accustomed to be either well-disposed or angry toward anyone." You will not win belief, of course, when you argue this; for he will see that they both are and have been angry with you.
passages.notes: "videbit" is presumably a misprint for "videbis" ("you will see") or for "videbuntur"; translated as "he will see", i.e. Caesar will see, which fits "non facies fidem". If "videbis" is read, the sense becomes "you will see that they both are and have been angry with you". Missing space in "irati.non" corrected.
